vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with severe, sudden-onset headache.
history_of_present_illness: He describes it as the 'worst headache of his life' (thunderclap headache) which started abruptly while he was lifting heavy boxes. It was associated with one episode of vomiting and photophobia.
physical_exam: Vitals: BP 160/95, HR 90, afebrile (37.1 C). Neurological exam: Awake, alert, oriented x3. Positive Brudzinski's and Kernig's signs indicating meningeal irritation. Pupils are equal, round, and reactive to light. No focal motor or sensory neurologic deficits.

test_results.labs: CBC, BMP, coagulation panel, and troponin are all within normal limits.
test_results.imaging: Non-contrast CT head: Hyperdensity in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissure, characteristic of acute subarachnoid hemorrhage. CT Angiography (CTA) brain: 6mm saccular aneurysm at the junction of the anterior communicating artery.
test_results.procedures: Lumbar puncture deferred due to positive CT head confirming SAH.

ground_truth: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) due to ruptured aneurysm
